DLEC-CTX-G1.title: ECON 214 Week 6 slides - Price elasticity of demand
DLEC-CTX-G1.text:
ECON 214 - Intermediate Microeconomics
Week 6 Lecture Slides: Price Elasticity of Demand
Prof. Adaeze Okonkwo-Hale | Harlow State University | Section 002

Slide 1 - Learning goals
- Compute own-price elasticity of demand using the course's midpoint convention
- Classify demand as elastic, inelastic, or unit elastic
- Connect elasticity to what happens to total revenue when price changes

Slide 2 - Definition
Own-price elasticity of demand measures how responsive quantity demanded is to a change in the good's own price:
E = (% change in quantity demanded) / (% change in price)
Because demand slopes down, the raw ratio is negative.

Slide 3 - ECON 214 convention (read this carefully)
In this course we ALWAYS use the midpoint (arc) formula unless a question explicitly says "point elasticity":
% change in Q = (Q2 - Q1) / ((Q1 + Q2) / 2)
% change in P = (P2 - P1) / ((P1 + P2) / 2)
We report own-price elasticity as an absolute value, rounded to two decimals. So you write 1.22, not -1.22.
Many textbooks (including the optional Marchetti text) divide by the starting values instead. That gives a different number for the same data, and it gives a different number depending on whether the price goes up or down. The midpoint version gives the same answer in both directions, which is why we use it.

Slide 4 - Classification (using the absolute value |E|)
- |E| > 1: elastic
- |E| < 1: inelastic
- |E| = 1 exactly: unit elastic
Note: 1.00 after rounding counts as unit elastic on problem sets and exams.

Slide 5 - Worked example: the Quad coffee cart
The coffee cart outside Benning Hall raises the price of a small drip coffee from $3.00 to $3.60. Daily sales fall from 500 cups to 400 cups.
Step 1: % change in Q = (400 - 500) / 450 = -0.2222, i.e. -22.2%
Step 2: % change in P = (3.60 - 3.00) / 3.30 = 0.1818, i.e. 18.2%
Step 3: E = -22.2% / 18.2% = -1.22
Step 4: report |E| = 1.22, so demand is elastic over this range.
Check: with the starting-value method you would get -20% / 20% = -1.00 and call it unit elastic. Same data, different classification. This is exactly why we fix one convention.

Slide 6 - Elasticity and total revenue
Total revenue TR = P x Q.
Before: $3.00 x 500 = $1,500 per day. After: $3.60 x 400 = $1,440 per day.
Rule: when demand is elastic, a price increase lowers total revenue; when demand is inelastic, a price increase raises total revenue; at unit elasticity total revenue does not change.
The coffee cart is consistent with the rule: elastic demand, price went up, revenue fell by $60 a day.

Slide 7 - What makes demand more elastic?
- Close substitutes are available (the dining hall sells drip coffee for $2.25)
- The good is a larger share of the budget
- A longer time horizon to adjust
- A narrowly defined market ("drip coffee at this cart" versus "caffeine")

Slide 8 - Exam notes
- Midterm 2 covers Weeks 5 to 8. Elasticity questions on Midterm 2 must use the midpoint formula; answers that use starting values get at most half credit.
- Show all four steps from Slide 5.
- The elasticity formula sheet is NOT provided on Midterm 2. Memorize the formulas.

Slide 9 - Preview of Week 7
Cross-price elasticity: the sign matters there (positive means substitutes, negative means complements), so we do NOT take absolute values for cross-price elasticity.

DLEC-CTX-G2.title: CS 261 Lecture 11 notes - Binary heaps and build-heap
DLEC-CTX-G2.text:
CS 261 - Data Structures
Lecture 11 Notes: Binary Heaps and Build-Heap
Prof. Tomasz Reinholt-Vega | Carrow Institute of Technology

1. What a binary heap is
A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array that satisfies the heap-order property. In CS 261 we use MIN-heaps by default: every node's key is less than or equal to the keys of its children, so the smallest key sits at the root.

2. CS 261 array convention (differs from the 0-indexed code you will see online)
We store the heap 1-indexed. Index 0 is left empty (we write it as _).
- parent(i) = floor(i / 2)
- left(i) = 2i
- right(i) = 2i + 1
If you see parent(i) = floor((i - 1) / 2) and left(i) = 2i + 1 online, that is the 0-indexed layout. Both are correct for their own layout, but on CS 261 quizzes you must use the 1-indexed formulas.

3. Height convention
In CS 261 the height of a tree counts NODES on the longest root-to-leaf path, so a single node has height 1 and an empty tree has height 0. (Most textbooks count edges, so for them a single node has height 0.) With our convention a heap with n keys has height floor(log2 n) + 1. Example: n = 7 gives height 3.

4. Sift-down (heapify at index i)
Compare the key at i with its children. If the smaller child is smaller than the key at i, swap with that smaller child and repeat from the child's index. Stop when the key is no larger than both children or when i has no children. Cost: O(height).

5. Build-heap (bottom-up)
Call sift-down on i = floor(n / 2), floor(n / 2) - 1, ..., 1. Leaves (indices greater than floor(n / 2)) are already heaps, so we skip them.
Total cost is O(n), not O(n log n). Most nodes live near the bottom and can only sift down a short distance; the sum of heights over all nodes is bounded by a linear function of n.

6. Worked example (show the array after every sift-down call; this is required on quizzes)
Input, n = 7: [_, 9, 4, 7, 1, 8, 2, 6]
Start at i = floor(7 / 2) = 3.
- sift-down(3): 7 vs children 2 (i=6) and 6 (i=7). Swap with 2. Array: [_, 9, 4, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6]
- sift-down(2): 4 vs children 1 (i=4) and 8 (i=5). Swap with 1. Index 4 has no children. Array: [_, 9, 1, 2, 4, 8, 7, 6]
- sift-down(1): 9 vs children 1 (i=2) and 2 (i=3). Swap with 1. Continue at i=2: 9 vs children 4 (i=4) and 8 (i=5). Swap with 4. Index 4 has no children. Array: [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]
Result: [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]. Four swaps total.

7. Other operations
- peek-min: O(1), it is A[1].
- insert: put the key at A[n + 1], then sift-up. O(log n).
- extract-min: move A[n] to A[1], shrink the heap, sift-down(1). O(log n).
- Finding the MAXIMUM in a min-heap is not cheap: the max is somewhere among the leaves, so it takes O(n) in general.

8. Logistics
Quiz 4 (next Thursday) covers heaps: sift-down traces, build-heap traces, and the index formulas above. Traces must use the 1-indexed layout. Priority queues and heapsort are on Quiz 5, not Quiz 4.
Office hours this week move to Wednesday 3-5 pm in Lowry 118 because of the department colloquium.

DLEC-CTX-I1.title: Rennick Library group study room policy
DLEC-CTX-I1.text:
Rennick Library - Group Study Room Policy (Fall Term)

Group study rooms on floors 2 and 3 of Rennick Library can be reserved by current students through the library booking portal. Each room holds between four and eight people and has a wall-mounted display and a whiteboard.

Booking rules
- Reservations open seven days in advance at 8:00 am.
- Each student may hold up to two hours of bookings per day and six hours per week.
- A room is released to the waitlist if nobody from the group checks in at the front desk within 15 minutes of the start time.
- Rooms 3B and 3C are quiet rooms: whiteboard work only, no calls or video meetings.

During exam weeks
- The daily limit drops to 90 minutes so more groups get a turn.
- Overnight booking between midnight and 7:00 am is available only on floor 2.

Care of rooms
- Wipe the whiteboard and take your rubbish with you when you leave.
- Food is not allowed; covered drinks are fine.
- Report broken displays or dried-out markers at the front desk or through the portal's "Report a problem" link.

Repeated no-shows (three in one term) suspend booking privileges for two weeks. Questions: ask at the Rennick front desk or contact the circulation team through the library website.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: Okay so most of the ATP in the cell comes from oxidative phosphorylation in the mitochondria, and that happens across the inner membrane, which is why the inner membrane is folded up into all these cristae.
items.answer: Right, and the folding matters because it packs a lot of inner membrane into a small space. The electron transport chain and ATP synthase sit in that membrane, so more surface area means more of those complexes working at once, which is why cells with high energy demand, like muscle and liver cells, tend to have more cristae. The gradient itself is a proton gradient across the inner membrane, and ATP synthase uses the flow of protons back across it to make ATP.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: why n/2?
conversation: USER (typed to Natively): she wrote T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Theta(n) for merge sort and I have no idea how to read that

NATIVELY: That's a **recurrence relation**. It's a compact way of saying how much work an algorithm does, written in terms of itself on a smaller input.

Read it piece by piece. T(n) is the total time to sort n items. The **2T(n/2)** means the algorithm splits the problem into 2 subproblems, each half the size. The **Theta(n)** is the extra work done at this level, outside the recursive calls, and for merge sort that's the merging step, which touches all n elements.

So merge sort sorts two halves of size n/2, then spends linear time merging them back together. You solve the recurrence with the master theorem or a recursion tree, and here it comes out to Theta(n log n).
items.answer:
The **n/2** is the size of each subproblem. Merge sort splits the array into two halves, so if the whole thing has n elements, each half has n/2. That's why the recursive part is 2T(n/2): two calls, each on half the input.

The n inside Theta(n) is different. That's the merge step, which touches all n elements at this level, not half of them. So the two numbers play different roles: n/2 is how big each piece is, n is how much work you do putting them back together.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: And this is why industry loves catalysts, right? You add a catalyst to the contact process and it pushes the equilibrium over toward sulfur trioxide, so you end up with a higher yield.
items.answer: That's the intuition, but it's not quite what a catalyst does. A catalyst speeds up the rate at which the reaction reaches equilibrium, it doesn't shift where the equilibrium sits. The position of equilibrium depends on temperature, pressure, and concentrations, not on the catalyst. So in the contact process, the catalyst gets you to the same equilibrium yield faster, which matters for throughput and economics, but it won't push the yield past what the equilibrium allows. To actually shift it toward sulfur trioxide you'd change conditions, like higher pressure or removing the product as it forms.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: using the slides' method, what's the elasticity if the cart cuts the price from 3.60 back to 3.00 and sales go from 400 back up to 500?
items.answer:
Using the midpoint formula, the price cut from $3.60 to $3.00 with sales rising from 400 to 500 gives the same **1.22**, elastic.

Step 1: % change in Q = (500 - 400) / 450 = 0.2222, so 22.2%.
Step 2: % change in P = (3.00 - 3.60) / 3.30 = -0.1818, so -18.2%.
Step 3: E = 22.2% / -18.2% = -1.22.
Step 4: report |E| = 1.22, so demand is elastic over this range.

That's the point of the midpoint convention: reversing the direction gives the same magnitude, unlike the starting-value method, which would give 25% / -16.7% = -1.50 here.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: Le Chatelier's principle: if you disturb a system at equilibrium, it shifts in the direction that partly undoes the disturbance.
items.answer: Le Chatelier's principle says a system at equilibrium reacts to a disturbance by shifting in whichever direction partially counteracts it. So if you add more of a reactant, the equilibrium moves toward the products to use some of it up. If you increase pressure by shrinking the volume, it shifts toward the side with fewer gas molecules. And if you raise the temperature, it shifts in the endothermic direction, the one that absorbs the added heat. The key idea is that the shift is only partial, it eases the disturbance without fully canceling it.

items.question: another one, different numbers
conversation: USER (typed to Natively): teach me build-heap properly using his worked example: why we start at floor(n/2), what each sift-down does to the array, and why the whole thing is O(n) and not O(n log n).

NATIVELY: Start at floor(n/2) because everything past that index is a leaf, and a single node is already a valid heap, so there's nothing to fix. Sift-down only matters for nodes with children.

In the example, n = 7, so we start at i = 3. Sift-down(3) swaps 7 with its smaller child 2, giving [_, 9, 4, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6]. Sift-down(2) swaps 4 with 1, giving [_, 9, 1, 2, 4, 8, 7, 6]. Sift-down(1) swaps 9 with 1, then continues down and swaps 9 with 4, giving [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]. Four swaps total.

It's O(n), not O(n log n), because most nodes sit near the bottom and can only sift a short distance. Summing each node's height over the whole tree stays linear in n.

NATIVELY: Start at floor(n/2) because everything after that index is a leaf, and a leaf is already a valid heap on its own, so there's nothing to fix. Sift-down only does work on nodes that have children.

In the example, n = 7, so we start at i = 3. Sift-down(3) swaps 7 with its smaller child 2, giving [_, 9, 4, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6]. Sift-down(2) swaps 4 with 1, giving [_, 9, 1, 2, 4, 8, 7, 6]. Sift-down(1) swaps 9 with 1, then keeps going and swaps 9 with 4, giving [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]. Four swaps total.

It's O(n) and not O(n log n) because most nodes sit near the bottom and can only sift a short distance. Add up each node's height across the whole tree and the total stays linear in n.
items.answer:
Same idea, fresh numbers. Take n = 6, array [_, 5, 3, 8, 1, 9, 2]. Start at floor(6/2) = 3, since indices 4, 5, 6 are leaves.

Sift-down(3): 8 has child 2, swap, giving [_, 5, 3, 2, 1, 9, 8]. Sift-down(2): 3's smaller child is 1, swap, giving [_, 5, 1, 2, 3, 9, 8]. Sift-down(1): 5's smaller child is 1, swap, then 5's smaller child is 3, swap again, giving [_, 1, 3, 2, 5, 9, 8]. Three swaps total.

Still O(n) because most nodes are near the bottom and sift only a short way. Add up each node's height and the total stays linear in n.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: Okay. So if you want the derivative of sine x from first principles, you write sine of x plus h, expand it with the angle addition formula, and the whole thing comes down to two limits: sine h over h, and cosine h minus one over h.
conversation: PROFESSOR: Before we start, quick housekeeping. The problem set deadline moved to Monday at noon because of the fire drill.
PROFESSOR: Also the Hendry Hall parking lot is closed this week, so give yourselves extra time.
items.answer:
The lecturer is walking through the first-principles derivation of the derivative of sine x. You start with the limit definition, write sin(x + h), and expand it with the angle addition formula:

sin(x + h) = sin x cos h + cos x sin h

Substituting that in and grouping terms gives sin x times (cos h − 1)/h plus cos x times (sin h)/h. As h goes to zero, sin h over h goes to 1 and (cos h − 1) over h goes to 0, so you're left with cos x. That's the two limits the lecturer named.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: And that's the same logic behind why cartels like the one we looked at last week keep falling apart.
conversation: PROFESSOR (heard): Classic prisoner's dilemma. Each prisoner does better by confessing no matter what the other one does, so they both confess, even though both staying quiet would leave them better off.

NATIVELY: The key idea is that confessing is a **dominant strategy**: it gives each prisoner a better outcome regardless of what the other does. If the other stays quiet, confessing means a lighter sentence. If the other confesses, confessing still beats staying quiet. So rational self-interest drives both to confess, and they land on a worse outcome than if they had both stayed quiet. That gap between individual rationality and collective benefit is the dilemma.

NATIVELY: That's the setup for an iterated prisoner's dilemma. When the game repeats indefinitely, the calculation changes: each player now has to weigh today's payoff against how the other will respond tomorrow. Cooperation can become rational, because defecting today invites retaliation in future rounds. The classic result is that a tit-for-tat strategy, cooperating first and then mirroring the other player's last move, tends to do well, since it rewards cooperation and punishes defection without escalating. So repetition is what makes sustained cooperation possible where a one-shot game drives both to confess.
items.answer: Cartels are a real-world iterated prisoner's dilemma. Each firm does better in the short run by undercutting the agreed price and grabbing market share, so cheating is tempting no matter what the others do. But because the game repeats, every firm knows that cheating today invites retaliation tomorrow, usually a price war that leaves everyone worse off. So the cartel holds together only as long as each member values future cooperation more than today's gain, and it tends to break down when that calculation flips, for instance when a firm is struggling and needs the short-term payoff, or when the members can't monitor each other well enough to detect and punish cheating.

Sift-down(1) swaps 9 with 1, then continues down and swaps 9 with 4, giving [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]. Four swaps total.

It's O(n), not O(n log n), because most nodes sit near the bottom and can only sift a short distance. Summing each node's height over the whole tree stays linear in n.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: whats entropy
items.answer:
Entropy is a measure of how many ways a system can be arranged without changing how it looks from the outside. A shuffled deck of cards has high entropy because there are so many orderings that all look equally random, while a sorted deck has low entropy because there's essentially one arrangement.

In information theory, Shannon entropy quantifies the average surprise in a message: H = -Σ p(x) log p(x), where p(x) is the probability of each outcome. A fair coin flip has one bit of entropy, a biased coin less, because the outcome is more predictable.

The intuition is that entropy is uncertainty. The more evenly spread the probabilities, the harder the outcome is to guess, and the more information you gain when you learn it.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: And the printing press is the key here, Gutenberg's from around 1450, which is why Luther's Ninety-five Theses in 1517 spread across the German lands in a matter of weeks.
items.answer: The printing press is what made that speed possible. Gutenberg's movable-type press, around 1450, let texts be reproduced in large numbers quickly and cheaply, so Luther's Ninety-five Theses in 1517 could be printed and copied across the German lands within weeks instead of being hand-copied over years. It's the classic case of a new communication technology accelerating an idea.

items.question: Quick check before we move on. If I give you a heap with twelve keys, what's its height? Use our convention, not the book's.
items.answer: With our convention, height counts nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path, so a heap with n keys has height floor(log2 n) + 1. For n = 12, floor(log2 12) is 3, so the height is **4**.

items.question: So in the trial the p-value came out at 0.03, and what that tells us is there's only a three percent chance the null hypothesis is true.
items.answer: That's a common misreading, actually. A p-value of 0.03 means that **if the null hypothesis were true**, there'd be a 3% chance of seeing data at least as extreme as what you got. It's the probability of the data given the null, not the probability of the null given the data. To get the chance the null is true, you'd need a Bayesian posterior, which also depends on your prior.

items.question: she wrote T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Theta(n) for merge sort and I have no idea how to read that
items.answer:
That's a **recurrence relation**. It's a compact way of saying how much work an algorithm does, written in terms of itself on a smaller input.

Read it piece by piece. T(n) is the total time to sort n items. The **2T(n/2)** means the algorithm splits the problem into 2 subproblems, each half the size. The **Theta(n)** is the extra work done at this level, outside the recursive calls, and for merge sort that's the merging step, which touches all n elements.

So merge sort sorts two halves of size n/2, then spends linear time merging them back together. You solve the recurrence with the master theorem or a recursion tree, and here it comes out to Theta(n log n).

items.question: she wrote upside-down A x, backwards E y, Loves(x, y) on the board, then wrote backwards E y, upside-down A x, Loves(x, y) and said they mean totally different things. what are those symbols, how do I read them out loud, and why does swapping the order change the meaning?
items.answer:
The upside-down A is the **universal quantifier**, read "for all." The backwards E is the **existential quantifier**, read "there exists."

So the first one, ∀x ∃y Loves(x, y), reads "for all x, there exists a y such that x loves y." Everyone loves someone. The second, ∃y ∀x Loves(x, y), reads "there exists a y such that for all x, x loves y." There's one person whom everyone loves.

The order matters because each quantifier's scope extends to everything after it. In the first, the y can be chosen per x, so it can differ for each person. In the second, the y is fixed first, so it has to be the same one for everybody.

items.question: But a lot of historians now call that the Westphalian myth. If you actually read the treaties, they say surprisingly little about sovereignty.
conversation: PROFESSOR (heard): So the Peace of Westphalia, 1648, ends the Thirty Years' War, and it's usually taught as the moment the modern system of sovereign states is born.

NATIVELY: The Peace of Westphalia is actually two treaties signed in 1648, in Münster and Osnabrück, that ended both the Thirty Years' War in the Empire and the Eighty Years' War between Spain and the Dutch Republic. Its reputation as the birth of the sovereign state system comes mainly from the idea of **cuius regio, eius religio** extended further, letting each territory's ruler settle religion, and from the way it treated the Empire's princes as having real standing of their own. Historians do push back on the "Westphalian sovereignty" story, since the treaties still left the Emperor and the Empire's institutions in place, and sovereignty as a formal doctrine came later, with Bodin and then the nineteenth century. So it's a useful marker, but more of a milestone than a clean break.
items.answer: That's the revisionist reading, and it's well supported. The treaties are mostly about specific grievances: confessional rights, territorial compensation, the Palatinate succession, amnesties, and the Empire's internal procedures like the Reichstag and the courts. Sovereignty in the abstract barely appears. What they do is confirm the Empire's constitutional structure rather than dissolve it, which is why scholars like Andreas Osiander argue the "Westphalian system" was read back into 1648 by nineteenth and twentieth century international lawyers. So the myth isn't that something happened in 1648, it's that the treaties created a doctrine of sovereignty they never actually state.
